definition: An agunah (chained wife — husband missing) appears as a character / her case is the subject.
The Angel of Death (מלאך המוות, סמאל) appears as an agent in the story.
Angels (מלאכים) appear in the story.
A baal shem (master of the Name) appears as a character — typically a pre-Hasidic figure or a non-Hasidic kabbalistic healer; NOT the Besht.
Demons / evil spirits (שדים, מזיקים) appear in the story.
Elijah the prophet appears as a character (in disguise, in dream, in revelation).
A nistar / hidden righteous person (often a lamed-vavnik) is a character.
A character who is a magician / wonder-worker (כושף, מכשף) — typically non-Jewish.
The messiah (משיח) appears in some role, or messianic expectations are central.
A maggid (preacher) appears as a distinct character — typically a different role than the rebbe.
A shochet (ritual slaughterer) appears as a character with some role.
Sabbatai Zevi or Sabbatean themes appear.
A character whose profession is sofer (scribe of Torah scrolls / amulets).
A character whose profession is tavern-keeper / innkeeper (אורנדאר, פונדקאי).
Members of the tzaddik's immediate family (wife, sons, daughters, parents) appear as characters.
A witch / female magician character appears.
Adultery (ניאוף) is at issue in the story.
A character is angry — typically as a moral failing or a heated moment.
Awe (יראה, יראת שמים) — religious awe of God or of a tzaddik.
Charity (צדקה) — giving alms, providing for the poor.
A character experiences fear (פחד, חרדה) — typically of God, of a tzaddik, of danger.
Humility (ענוה) as a depicted/discussed virtue.
Joy (שמחה) as a depicted state, often religious — joy in serving God, joy on a holiday.
Lust / desire (תאוה) is at issue.
Lying / deception by a character.
Pride / arrogance (גאוה) as a moral failing.
Religious / moral prohibitions (אסור) are at issue in the story — typically a character is told not to do something, or violates a prohibition.
A character is punished for wrongdoing (often by Heaven, sometimes by the tzaddik).
Repentance (teshuvah) is depicted — a character turns from sin.
A character resists a temptation (lust, profit, fame).
Sadness / melancholy (עצבות, מרה שחורה) — typically as a spiritual problem the story addresses.
A character is shamed (בושה) — typically as a spiritual or social consequence.
A general/unspecified virtue is at issue. Often the story's point is to illustrate one.
A character experiences devekut — mystical cleaving / communion with God.
A character has a dream that is depicted in the story (and typically matters for the plot — revelation, warning, etc.).
A character experiences hitlahavut — religious enthusiasm/burning fervor.
Aliyat neshamah — ascent of the soul / journey to upper worlds while alive.
A character experiences a revelation (giluy) — direct mystical/supernatural disclosure.
A character trembles (רעד, חרדה) — physical trembling as religious or supernatural response.
A character sees visions — supernatural sights in waking state.
Story whose narrative is the first encounter / 'finding' of a tzaddik — a neutral character discovers him.
Story about the birth of a tzaddik — typically miraculous circumstances.
Story whose central narrative is the death of a tzaddik (deathbed scene, last teachings, succession).
Story whose central event is a tzaddik's inauguration as rebbe.
Story that is structured as a parable / mashal told BY a tzaddik (not a story ABOUT a tzaddik).
Story whose narrative arc is a prediction/prophecy by a tzaddik that comes true.
Story whose central narrative is the tzaddik protecting someone from danger (illness, hostile authorities, demons).
Story whose narrative arc is rapprochement: an outsider/skeptic is drawn close to a tzaddik / Hasidism through the events of the story.
Story whose narrative is the revelation (giluy) of a hidden tzaddik to others or himself.
Story whose point is to illustrate the virtues (humility, charity, faith, etc.) of a tzaddik.

Use of Lurianic kavvanot (כוונות) — mystical intentions assigned to specific words of prayer or ritual actions. The story depicts a character praying/acting WITH explicit kavvanot, or discusses kavvanot as a kabbalistic concept. NOT generic 'good intention' (כוונה טובה) in a non-mystical sense.

Use of Lurianic yihudim (יחודים, ייחודים) — mystical 'unifications' of divine names or sefirot performed contemplatively, typically by a tzaddik or kabbalist. NOT the marital-seclusion sense of יחוד (a couple alone together), and NOT a generic call to monotheistic unity.
Esoteric / hidden knowledge (תורת הסוד, נסתר) — kabbalah, mystical doctrines, knowledge accessible only to initiates.
Practical kabbalah (קבלה מעשית) — use of mystical knowledge to effect concrete results (amulets, healings, manipulation of names/spirits).
Possession, transmission, or use of secret/hidden manuscripts (כתבים, כתבי הסוד) — typically kabbalistic.

Applies when the text is mainly halakhic: a ruling, a legal question and its answer, a codification of practice, or the rationale for a custom presented as law rather than as narrated events. Attribution to a Hasidic master does not make it a story. Distinguish from :sermon, which is homiletic or exegetical rather than legal.

Applies when the story praises the holiness, piety, wisdom or wonders of a figure outside the Hasidic movement: an earlier or non-Hasidic sage, kabbalist or rabbinic authority such as the Ari, the Hida, the Maharal's circle, the author of Gur Aryeh, R. Shimshon of Vienna, or a pious man taken from an older book. Such stories are often explicitly copied from earlier works. A tale about a Hasidic tsaddik does not qualify, even if it is laudatory.

Applies when the text is mainly homiletic or exegetical teaching rather than narrated events. Examples are interpretations of verses or prayers, gematria and kabbalistic explanations, rationales for customs, and ethical discourses, often introduced as sayings 'from the holy rabbi'. It also applies when a narrative is wrapped in an extended homiletic or justificatory frame. Attribution of the teaching to a Hasidic master does not make it a story.

Applies when the text's declared purpose is moral instruction in a particular virtue, such as humility, charity and lovingkindness, or hospitality. This holds whether the text is an exemplary tale (often about pre-Hasidic figures or hidden righteous men, framed with 'from this we learn') or a short ethical teaching. A story that merely depicts a virtuous character, without being framed as a lesson in that virtue, does not suffice.
Ascetic self-denial: abstaining from food, prolonged fasts, mortification, separation from one's wife, or rigorous austerity, including debate over whether such practices are proper.
A tsaddik advises someone on livelihood or commerce, such as taking or refusing a lease (ארענדע), abandoning a trade, or handling dealings with a nobleman.
A brit milah (ברית מילה) appears in the story, whether as a ceremony, the honours of sandak or mohel, the festive meal, or the eve of the circumcision (וואך נאכט) as the setting.
Clothing with religious or social significance, such as white Sabbath garments, a hat worn askew, or a tsaddik's refusal to change his dress.
Struggling with or dispelling stray, distracting thoughts (מחשבות זרות) during prayer or devotion, including teachings on how to handle them.

Dancing (ריקוד) as a depicted activity, such as hasidim dancing in a circle on Simhat Torah, a tsaddik leaping and dancing during prayer, or dancing at a wedding or festive meal. Playful movement or merriment without dancing does not suffice.
Cleaving to God (דביקות): a person shown in a state of rapt attachment, ecstatic worship, or absorption in God, during prayer, at the table, or in solitude.
Drinking wine or spirits as a depicted act, whether at a meal, in a toast or blessing, or as an occasion for a wonder or a lesson.
A tsaddik's prediction, intercession, remedy, or segulah fails or does not work as expected, along with the explanation given for the failure.
Fasting (תענית) as a depicted practice, such as fasting from Sabbath to Sabbath or eating once a week. This includes a tsaddik's criticism of excessive fasting.
A point of Jewish law is raised or decided in the story, such as testing someone on a legal ruling, or an action justified by a halakhic principle.

Physical healing of the sick, whether by the tsaddik's prayer, touch, remedies, amulets, or instructions, or as a stated habit of healing. It includes cases where doctors have failed and the tsaddik succeeds.
Spiritual rather than bodily healing: a tsaddik repairs (תיקון) a person's soul, reveals the sins someone must mend, redeems a transmigrated soul, or draws a person to repentance and holiness.
A tsaddik makes a jest or witty remark (מילתא דבדיחותא), or treats a serious matter jokingly.
A tsaddik saves a person from imminent or foretold death, such as reviving a dying or dead child, rescuing someone from a predicted drowning, or driving off the angel of death from a sick man.
Contemplative mystical concentration: performing yihudim, prayer with kavanot, deep contemplation (עמקות), or night vigils of inner worship.
Singing or music-making as a depicted activity: a tsaddik singing zemirot or Lekha Dodi, chanting praises in ecstasy, or music at a wedding.
Redemption of a soul: a tsaddik intervenes to avert death or a heavenly decree hanging over a person, or a pidyon payment is given to the tsaddik for that purpose.

Ransoming captives (פדיון שבויים), meaning efforts to free Jews who are imprisoned, held captive, or arrested. This includes travelling to collect money for ransom and appealing to a tsaddik to secure a prisoner's release.

Visiting or prostrating at the grave of a tsaddik, or the burial and tomb of a tsaddik shown as a site of reverence. This includes deathbed instructions about one's burial that frame the grave as a holy place.

Prayer (תפילה) as a depicted activity — formal recitation of liturgy. No separate halakhic-prayer tag; the practice tag covers both depicted and discussed prayer (Chen flagged the overlap; resolved by collapsing the halakhah branch).
A tsaddik shields individuals or communities from harm: demons and spirits, hostile noblemen, blood libels, decrees, or other dangers, through prayer, presence, rebuke, or ritual means.
The tsaddik receives visitors or followers at his court: granting or refusing an audience, greeting newcomers, testing a would-be follower, or sending a hasid away.
Reciting Psalms (תהלים) as a depicted practice, such as a tsaddik saying Psalms from a book during hardship, or Psalms said as a form of devotion or intercession.
Ransoming or attempting to free captive or imprisoned Jews (פדיון שבויים); a duplicate of practice:pidyon_shvuyim with the same scope.
Freeing an aguna, a woman whose husband has disappeared, so that she may remarry, typically by establishing or revealing the husband's death or whereabouts.
Ritual slaughter (שחיטה) and its institutions: the shohet, learning or certifying slaughter, inspecting the knife, or dismissing an unfit shohet.
A homily or Torah discourse (דרשה, דברי תורה) delivered or quoted in the story, including exegesis of verses presented as the tsaddik's teaching and preachers giving sermons.
Sexual abstinence (פרישות), whether separation from one's wife undertaken as a vow or practice, celibacy after a wife's death, or a vow of abstinence and its violation.
Smoking, typically the tsaddik smoking his pipe (לולקע), shown as a habitual or meaningful act: a moment of concentration, preparation before prayer, or a puzzle to onlookers.
Seclusion (התבודדות): withdrawing to a forest, cave, or private room to worship alone, or living shut away from society.

Telling stories as a depicted practice. A tsaddik or hasid narrates a tale at a gathering or festive meal, or the text frames the story as told by a named tsaddik on a set occasion; this includes telling stories as a spiritual or theurgic act, such as praying for the sick through stories.
Torah study as a depicted activity: learning Talmud or Kabbalah, pilpul, a teacher studying with pupils, or a scholar devoting his days to learning.
Tefillin appear in the story: wearing them (including unusual customs such as two pairs), their protective power, or examining and finding them invalid.

The tsaddik himself journeys from place to place (with disciples, wandering, passing through towns, lodging with innkeepers or leaseholders), and the story turns on the journey or his stay en route. Hasidim travelling to the tsaddik belong under travel_to_the_tsaddik.
The doctrine of the tsaddik as a theme: the need to cleave to and receive from a true tsaddik, faith in the tsaddik as faith in God, or the tsaddik's power to intercede and act on others' behalf.
A disciple or tsaddik goes to a tsaddik other than his own master, often after the master's death or on his instruction, or seeks out another tsaddik while passing through a town.

A hasid or seeker journeys to a tsaddik's court, whether to see him, learn from him, spend Sabbath or holidays with him, or bring a request. A mention of discipleship without a journey does not suffice.
Ritual immersion in a mikveh or river (טבילה), as a depicted act or habit, such as going to the mikveh before Sabbath or prayer, or building a mikveh.

Practical use of holy names: adjurations (השבעות), combinations of divine names, the ascent of the soul by adjuration, or name-based feats such as shortening the road (קפיצת הדרך) and wresting a secret from Samael. Amulets are tagged here only when their power is explicitly tied to holy names.
Writing or using amulets (קמיעות) or protective inscriptions (שמירות), including the conditions under which they were written and the loss or restoration of their efficacy.
Competition between two tzaddikim, or between a tzaddik and a rival.
Conflict — typically the tzaddik in conflict with an antagonist (Jewish opponent, non-Jew, demon).
Conversion to Judaism (or apostasy from it) is at issue.
A character disobeys an instruction — usually from the tzaddik, with consequences.
Divorce is depicted or at issue.
Excommunication (חרם, נדה) imposed on someone.
Interaction among Hasidim — not specifically the master-disciple relationship.
Conflict specifically between two tzaddikim (rebbes).
Succession of leadership from one rebbe to the next (usually father-to-son).
The relationship between a Hasidic master (rebbe) and his disciple is central.
The marital relationship between two characters (typically a married couple) is depicted.
Marriage — the event, or the institution as the subject.
Poverty embraced as a virtue (typically the tzaddik refusing wealth, or living in voluntary poverty).
Interaction with mitnagdim / non-Hasidic Jews (typically maskilim or opponents).
Interaction with non-Jews (גוים, ערלים) — including nobles, peasants, priests, etc.
Interaction with Jewish sinners (averyianim) — the tzaddik reaching out, drawing back, judging.
Interaction with state authorities — government officials, governors, the Tsar, etc.

A character belatedly realizes the truth about another character or situation — e.g. a stranger turning out to be the tzaddik, but also any other retrospective recognition (someone was righteous, someone was a sinner, an event had hidden meaning, etc.).
A beit midrash or yeshiva (study hall) is a setting in the story.
Heaven / upper worlds (שמים, גן עדן, היכלות) appears in the story as a SETTING — the action happens there, or a character ascends.
Hell / gehinnom / the punishment-realm appears as a setting.
The hasidic court (חצר הצדיק, חצר) — the rebbe's residence/community space.
A mikveh (ritual bath) is a setting in the story — a scene takes place there.
A rabbinical court (בית דין) is a setting — legal/halakhic proceedings.
The Land of Israel (ארץ ישראל, א״י, ירושלים, צפת, חברון) is the setting or the destination of travel.
A character communicates with invisible beings — angels, souls, voices from heaven (bat kol), etc.
Kefitzat ha-derekh — miraculous contraction of distance / fast travel.
Light or fire appears around a character as a sign of his righteousness (typical: Torah-study illuminated by celestial fire).
Magic / sorcery (כישוף) — performed by witches, non-Jewish magicians, or Jews using forbidden practices.

A miracle (נס / מופת) is depicted as a discrete supernatural event with a clear before/after — typically attached to the recipient of the intervention. Excludes ambient miraculousness (tzaddik perceives at a distance, etc.) and magical acts by a magician (use supernatural:magic).
A character perceives supernaturally — sees things others can't, knows things he couldn't know normally (ruach hakodesh).
Miraculous / supernatural pregnancy or conception (typically: a childless woman conceives via a tzaddik's blessing).
A character (typically a tzaddik) predicts a future event that comes true.
Reincarnation (gilgul) of a soul is depicted or central to the plot.
A birth is a depicted event in the story (typically the birth of a future tzaddik, or of a child whose birth required a miracle).
A death is a depicted event in the story (of a tzaddik, a relative, an antagonist, etc.).
Eschatological events / end-of-days themes — coming of messiah, end-times signs, world-to-come (עולם הבא).
A historical event is part of the story's setting (a war, a decree, a famous gathering).
The story takes place on a Jewish holiday (Pesach, Sukkot, Yom Kippur, Rosh Hashana, Purim, Chanukah, etc.).
Inauguration / installation of a tzaddik as rebbe of a community (kabbalat malkhut, accepting leadership).
The story takes place on / centers on Shabbat (שבת קודש, ערב שבת, מוצאי שבת).
A woman triggers the plot or is the reason for events, without being a central actor.
A woman is a central actor in the story with her own agency.
A woman is referred to but does not act in the narrative.
A woman appears in a small or peripheral role and acts in the narrative.
